Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 30
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Tax Inspector
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Car Similarity: Similar cars
  Maladaptive Strategies: Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking, Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping, Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again

Vignette:
Tariq had been driving home from a site visit when a delivery truck swerved, forcing him to brake hard. The car behind him had not, and the impact sent his sedan spinning across two lanes before it struck a concrete barrier. Metal screamed, glass shattered, and a ruptured liquor bottle from a nearby truck sprayed its contents across the windshield. When the world stopped turning, he sat in the wreckage, certain he would not walk away. The event lodged in him not as a single memory, but as a collection of sensory facts that continued to demand attention. In the weeks that followed, the trauma replayed in fragments that seized him without warning. He found himself flinching whenever he saw cars collide on the street or hear tires screech at the next intersection. A similar silver sedan parked too close to his building’s lot made him step back, his chest tightening as if the impact were imminent. What frightened him most was the smell of alcohol drifting from a street vendor’s cart or a colleague’s breath; it carried him instantly back to the spilled liquor pooling across his dashboard. He was certain those sensory moments were not just echoes, but active reminders that the road remained dangerous. His body had become a listening post. Tariq reported being perpetually on guard, his attention sharpened to the point where a dropped pen, a sudden phone notification, or a contractor’s hammer outside made him jump. He was watchful, waiting for the next shock, and he could not explain why ordinary noises felt like threats. His symptom burden, measured at a moderate thirty-five, settled into his daily rhythm without overwhelming it. His avoidance habits formed alongside his mounting alertness. He avoided driving whenever possible, taking the bus or walking even when the distance warranted a car. When he rode as a passenger, he gripped the door handle, his eyes fixed on the flow of traffic. At his municipal desk, where he reviewed property assessments as a tax inspector, he spent long hours on his phone, playing games or scrolling through feeds to keep his mind occupied. He was not tired from the screen itself, but from the effort of using it as a shelter against the thoughts that rose when he was still. His food restriction developed in parallel; he began skipping lunch, picking at meals, and limiting his portions until eating felt like a manageable, predictable routine. His professional environment provided the ground for these habits. While cross-referencing tax codes at his desk, he noticed how easily his focus fractured when the office printer jammed or a clerk called out across the floor. He remained on guard, and the quiet office offered few distractions. His occupation, once a source of confidence, stood as a mirror for his interpretations. He prided himself on precision, yet he caught himself second-guessing calculations he had once made effortlessly. He could not rely on himself, he realized, when the numbers blurred or when a client’s dispute demanded a quick, decisive read. He felt no longer capable of doing the things that had defined him—navigating audit sites without hesitation, managing a caseload without exhaustion. What worried him most was the emotional quiet that had settled over him. He knew he felt things, but the feelings seemed distant, muffled beneath a layer of static. He had come to believe he would never be able to feel normal emotions again, that the crash had taken something permanent. The decision to seek help came on a Tuesday. A routine property inspection had turned into a long wait in a cramped municipal vehicle while a surveyor worked. When the car door slammed, Tariq startled, his heart hammering, and he realized he had eaten almost nothing since morning. He stayed on the bus that day, opening a game on his phone as the city blurred past, feeling the familiar pull of avoidance. He was ready to try something different, hoping to reclaim his footing without surrendering to the fear, though he remained wary of whether his doubts and the quiet inside him would ever lift.
